newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists say "Yes, but" to euro.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists say "Yes, but" to euro.

text.p: France's main opposition Socialist party confirmed on Friday it was committed to European monetary union, but only under certain conditions, including early membership by Italy, Spain, and Britain.
In its official manifesto for a two-round parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, the party noted that the new euro was due to be launched on January 1, 1999.
"We say yes to the switch to the euro, but under certain conditions," it said.

"The creation of the euro must not exclude founding members of Europe, nor those which have become pillars of the European Union. We want the single currency to belong to all of the European Union," it said.
"Membership by Italy and Spain seems to us necessary and possible, as well as by Britain, if it wants it," it added.
The manifesto said Europe, when deciding which countries qualify to join, must take account of the trend shown towards meeting Maastricht treaty criteria, as allowed for in the treaty itself.

European ministers generally refuse to say in advance of a decision due in April/May 1998 which countries will qualify for the euro, saying it depends on how well they fulfil Maastricht treaty criteria.
And nor do they want to be drawn on exactly how Maastricht criteria will be interpreted, though Germany is expected to lead those calling for a strict interpretation of the treaty.

The Socialist party also called for a "solidarity and growth pact" in Europe, instead of an "austerity pact" -- an apparent reference to the stability pact agreed by EU leaders last year to limit budget deficits after the launch of the euro.

It was unclear, however, whether this meant renegotiating the stabilty pact, an idea likely to be rejected by most of France's partners in Europe, which spent months last year agreeing on how powerful they should make this pact.
The Socialist party added that there must be a European economic government alongside the future European Central Bank.

Other EU countries have already rejected setting up such a government -- an idea floated by some French politicians last year. But they have agreed, however, to an informal "stability council" to co-ordinate economic policies inside the euro zone.
The Socialist party, echoing calls made by the government, insisted the new euro must not be overvalued against the dollar and the yen.
"To build the necessary monetary stability, exchange rates between major currencies must be balanced. We must prevent any form of monetary dumping," it said.
"We do not want a euro which is overvalued against the dollar and the yen," it said.
The Socialist party, which is trailing the centre-right coalition in opinion polls, has not spelled out what would happen if its conditions were not met.
But Socialist economic policy maker Dominique Strauss-Kahn said in an interview published on Friday that the party wanted the euro to be launched on time on January 1, 1999.
"We want to carry on building Europe and therefore we want a single currency to be launched at the planned time," Strauss-Kahn said in an interview with daily La Tribune.
"But this currency has to have a purpose. Nothing would be worse than taking this step without the European people feeling the slightest improvement in their situation," he said.
